				EU targets Russian ex-soldiers, banks and sports in new sanctions push			
							
				Brussels wants to restrict visas for former Russian soldiers, target banks and crypto platforms and bar Russian athletes from competing in the EU.

					AI generated Text-to-speech

							Copied						
																					
									
											
											
																
							


						
																					
							Share via email						
																
									
											
											
																
							



						
																					
							Share on X

				Free article usually reserved for subscribers			
					
	
				
					
						

							
					
						Russian navy cadets march during a rehearsal for the Victory Day military parade at Dvortsovaya Square in St. Petersburg on April 23, 2026. | Olga Maltseva/AFP via Getty Images					
				
			
					
				
		
			
			
	
			
			November 23, 2026		
	
			
			5:15 pm CET		
	
	
		
	
	
	
	
	

	
	By 
			
			Koen Verhelst		
	

	
					
	
							

							
																																	
BRUSSELS — The EU wants to target former Russian soldiers, banks, crypto platforms and sports teams in its 22nd sanctions package against Moscow since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen announced on Monday.

“We’re giving Ukraine the strength to secure a peace. And Russia, every reason to choose it,” von der Leyen said in a prerecorded video message launching the package.

The Commission’s proposals will now be negotiated by EU countries, with several diplomats telling POLITICO that they aim to reach an agreement by the end of the year.

One major measure would restrict visas for former Russian soldiers. The EU agreed on a legal framework for the restrictions in its previous sanctions package over the summer but has yet to put them into effect.

“Russian ex-combatants pose a security risk to Europe. They cannot be allowed to wander freely across our countries,” von der Leyen said, citing a recent escalation in covert Russian operations in Europe.

The Commission also wants to add 70 vessels to its sanctions list targeting Russia’s so-called shadow fleet, which Moscow uses to export oil and other commodities.

European companies would also be barred from repairing Russian refineries damaged by Ukrainian drone attacks. EU citizens would no longer be allowed to sit on the boards of Russian companies.

On sports, the Commission is proposing to bar Russian teams and athletes from competing in the bloc, a move that would prevent Russia from returning to next year’s ice hockey world championship in Germany.

“We propose to ban the display of official Russian symbols. We will also restrict financial flows from Russian sponsors to European based sports and cultural associations,” von der Leyen said.

An arbitration court had ruled that the International Ice Hockey Federation lacked sufficient grounds to exclude Russia from the tournament.

Closing sanctions loopholes and cracking down on shadow finance is another focus of the package. The Commission wants to disconnect 60 more banks from international payment systems and target cryptocurrency and payment networks used to circumvent sanctions.

“We will focus on Russia, but also include third countries that help Russia to evade our sanctions,” von der Leyen said.

The EU has previously been cautious about directly targeting third countries, but von der Leyen said the new measures would help “align with international partners.”

The latest proposals follow a difficult year for EU sanctions policy. A previous package was held up for weeks over restrictions on liquefied natural gas shipments, while France delayed the renewal of an existing sanctions framework over a national security dispute, demanding the removal of two Russian billionaires from the sanctions list.

Last week, the Commission announced the creation of a dedicated sanctions office to oversee the design, drafting and coordination of restrictive measures.
